title: Describe, interpret and represent mathematical patterns, functions and algebra in different contexts

lessons.title: Number patterns in everyday farm work
lessons.html:
What is a pattern?

A pattern is something that repeats or changes by a fixed rule. When you find the rule, you can work out what comes next. Patterns are everywhere on a farm.

Repeating patterns

The feeding routine is a repeating pattern: feed at 6:00, 12:00 and 17:00, then again tomorrow at 6:00, 12:00 and 17:00. The farrier visits every 6 weeks. The pattern repeats.

Growing patterns

Some patterns grow by the same amount each time.

Example: each stable needs 2 buckets of water a day.

Stables12345
Buckets246810

The rule is: buckets = 2 × number of stables. Each time we add a stable, we add 2 buckets.

Finding the rule

Look at how much the numbers change each step.

Example: 5, 8, 11, 14, ... Each number is 3 more than the one before. The next numbers are 17 and 20.

Example: a foal's weight in the first weeks (made-up numbers for practice): 50 kg, 60 kg, 70 kg, 80 kg. The rule is +10 kg each week. If the rule stays the same, next week is 90 kg.

Patterns that start somewhere

Sometimes there is a fixed amount plus a growing amount. A transport company charges R500 to come out, plus R20 for every kilometre.

Kilometres0102030
Cost (R)5007009001 100

Rule: cost = 500 + 20 × kilometres. For 50 km: 500 + 20 × 50 = 500 + 1 000 = R1 500.

Why patterns help

When you know the rule you can plan: how much feed for more horses, how much a trip will cost, when the next vet visit is due. You do not have to count everything one by one.

lessons.title: Simple rules, formulas and graphs
lessons.html:
Using letters for numbers

In algebra we use a letter to stand for a number we do not know yet, or a number that can change. This makes a rule short and easy to write.

If each horse eats 3 kg of concentrate a day and h is the number of horses, then:

Feed (kg) = 3 × h, often written as 3h.

For 8 horses: 3 × 8 = 24 kg a day.

Input and output

Think of a rule as a machine. You put a number in (input), the rule works on it, and a number comes out (output). This is called a function.

Input: horses (h)Rule: 3hOutput: kg feed
23 × 26
53 × 515
103 × 1030

Working backwards

Sometimes you know the output and want the input. "We have 36 kg of feed. How many horses can we feed for one day?"

3h = 36, so h = 36 ÷ 3 = 12 horses.

To work backwards, do the opposite: the opposite of multiply is divide, the opposite of add is subtract.

Drawing a graph

We can show a rule on a graph. Put the input along the bottom (horizontal axis) and the output up the side (vertical axis). Plot each pair from the table as a dot. For the rule 3h the dots make a straight line going up. A straight line means the output grows by the same amount each time.

Reading a graph

To read a graph, find your input on the bottom, go straight up to the line, then go across to read the output. Graphs help supervisors see quickly how feed, cost or time changes.

Practice

A groom earns R25 for each extra horse she clips. Rule: pay = 25n. If she clips 6 horses: 25 × 6 = R150. If she earned R200: n = 200 ÷ 25 = 8 horses.

Always check your answer: put it back into the rule and see if it works.

Key points

  • A pattern changes by a fixed rule; find the change from one step to the next.
  • A letter can stand for a number that changes, such as h for horses.
  • A function takes an input and gives an output using a rule.
  • Work backwards by doing the opposite operation.
  • A rule that adds the same amount each time makes a straight-line graph.
